rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph's brothers came to buy wheat from the reserves he had accumulated during the seven plentiful years; famine had struck nearby countries, while Egypt alone had surplus under his personal distribution.
rows.anchor: to buy wheat from the stores which Joseph had accumulated during the seven years of plenty

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Benjamin was Joseph's full brother but the other ten brothers' paternal half-brother; Rachel was their mother, while the others had different mothers.
rows.anchor: Benjamin, who was Joseph's full brother

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Benjamin was Jacob's youngest child and had not joined the first trip to Egypt; Asad supposes the brothers had mentioned him to Joseph in conversation.
rows.anchor: Benjamin, the youngest of Jacob's children, had not accompanied his brothers on their first journey to Egypt

rows.speaker: Ibn Kathir
rows.claim: The returned merchandise was the goods the brothers had bartered for wheat.
rows.anchor: goods which they had bartered for wheat (Ibn Kathir): a very plausible explanation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad finds the barter explanation plausible because barter was the most common form of trade in ancient times.
rows.anchor: barter was the most common form of trade in those ancient times

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad renders the phrase as the brothers perceiving the returned goods when they reach their family, prompting them to return.
rows.anchor: so that they may perceive them when they come back to their family, [and] that they may return

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Measure is used metonymically for grain, recalling Joseph's warning in verse 60 that the brothers would receive no more measure unless Benjamin came.
rows.anchor: measure [of grain]", here used metonymically in an allusion to Joseph's words (verse 60)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad gives the literal sense of Jacob's question as asking whether he should trust them other than as he had trusted them before.
rows.anchor: Lit., "not otherwise than".

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph apparently allotted one camel-load of grain to each foreign buyer.
rows.anchor: Joseph used to allot to foreign buyers of grain one camel-load per person

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jacob advised separate gates probably to avoid attracting attention in the foreign land and becoming vulnerable to intrigue.
rows.anchor: Probably in order not to attract undue attention in the foreign land and possibly fall prey to intrigues

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The narrative shows that Jacob and his sons still had severe distress to endure before their story reached a happy outcome.
rows.anchor: they and their father were to suffer severe distress before their adventures came to a happy conclusion

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jacob's advice came from an understandable human wish to protect his sons; he did not expect outward precautions alone to change what God decreed.
rows.anchor: he followed only an instinctive, humanly - understandable urge, and did not really expect that any outward precaution would by itself help them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage underscores Islam's fundamental teaching that people depend wholly on God, explaining why the otherwise story-irrelevant advice appears here.
rows.anchor: This stress on man's utter dependence on God - a fundamental tenet of Islam - explains why Jacob's advice

rows.speaker: Zamakhshari
rows.claim: Asad's interpolated clause about Jacob's knowledge follows Zamakhshari's interpretation of the reference to Jacob being endowed with knowledge.
rows.anchor: based on Zamakhshari's interpretation of the above reference to Jacob's having been "endowed with knowledge"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Against the Biblical account, the Qur'an says Joseph disclosed his identity to Benjamin well before revealing himself to the ten half-brothers.
rows.anchor: contrary to the Biblical account, Joseph is stated here to have disclosed his identity to Benjamin

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reference to their past deeds means the brothers' treachery against Joseph, which he had presumably told Benjamin about.
rows.anchor: The words "their past doings" obviously refer to their treacherous behaviour towards himself

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mu'adhdhin means an announcer and derives from adhdhana, meaning to announce, proclaim, or call out publicly.
rows.anchor: "an announcer" (mu'adhdhin) - a noun derived from the verbal form adhdhana

rows.speaker: Razi
rows.claim: Razi argues the Qur'an never says Joseph ordered the accusation; servants likely suspected Jacob's sons themselves because nobody else had been near the cup.
rows.anchor: Razi says: "Nowhere in the Qur'an is it stated that they made this accusation on Joseph's orders

rows.speaker: Tabari and Zamakhshari
rows.claim: Tabari and Zamakhshari advance views like Razi's in explaining the final words of verse 76.
rows.anchor: Analogous views are also advanced by Tabari and Zamakhshari in their comments on the last words of verse 76 below

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad rejects the Biblical account that the false accusation was part of a contrivance devised by Joseph, finding the servants' independent suspicion more plausible.
rows.anchor: This extremely plausible explanation contrasts sharply with the Biblical account of this incident

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad supposes Joseph secretly put the royal cup in Benjamin's bag as a gift, without telling the servants, to conceal his special preference for Benjamin.
rows.anchor: had placed the royal cup as a present in the bag of his favourite brother; and that he did this secretly

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The literal wording says they spoke while turning toward the herald and his companions.
rows.anchor: Lit., "They said, turning towards them"

rows.speaker: Most of the commentators
rows.claim: Most commentators take the brothers' answer as stating that theft was customarily punished by enslavement among the ancient Hebrews, perhaps following Exodus 22:3.
rows.anchor: Most of the commentators (relying, perhaps on Exodus xxii, 3) assume that this was the customary punishment for theft among the ancient Hebrews

rows.speaker: Razi
rows.claim: Razi suggests the closing sentence may be the Egyptian herald's confirmation of Egyptian punishment, rather than part of the brothers' answer.
rows.anchor: Razi, however, suggests that this last sentence may not be a part of the brothers' answer but a confirmatory remark

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase literally means that Joseph brought the cup out of Benjamin's bag.
rows.anchor: Lit., "he brought it out".

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The episode illustrates that what happens rests with God alone, the same doctrine Jacob stated earlier.
rows.anchor: a further illustration of the basic doctrine that "judgment [as to what is to happen] rests with none but God"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Egyptian law and the brothers' guardianship and pledge prevented Joseph from keeping Benjamin; he was not ready to reveal his identity, so he otherwise had to let Benjamin leave.
rows.anchor: under the law of Egypt he could not do this without the consent of his half-brothers, who were the legal guardians

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The cup's unexpected discovery made Benjamin appear guilty, allowing Joseph to claim him under local law; the outcome was neither planned nor foreseen by Joseph.
rows.anchor: indicate that its final outcome was neither planned nor even foreseen by Joseph

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The brothers meant Joseph, his full brother, and likely slandered him to distance themselves from Benjamin despite having no evidence Joseph had stolen.
rows.anchor: it is reasonable to assume that the brothers, unaware of the fact that they were standing before Joseph, simply wanted to vilify him

rows.speaker: almost all the commentators
rows.claim: Most commentators take the pronoun it to refer to Joseph's ensuing unspoken saying or thought, signaled by the following verb he said.
rows.anchor: According to almost all the commentators, the pronoun "it" refers to Joseph's subsequent "saying" or, rather, thought

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad therefore renders the phrase freely to make clear that Joseph said this inwardly.
rows.anchor: hence my free rendering of this phrase

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The literal phrase means what they attribute to Joseph and Benjamin; Asad takes it as an allusion to the brothers having stolen Joseph from his father.
rows.anchor: Lit., "of what you attribute", i.e., to Joseph and Benjamin - sc., "since you yourselves have stolen Joseph from his father"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Though the word literally means know, the expression here denotes remembrance, which Asad renders as remember.
rows.anchor: since this expression denotes here remembrance rather than knowledge in the proper sense of the word

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's judgment in the eldest brother's favor means enabling him to win Benjamin back.
rows.anchor: enables me to win back my brother Benjamin

rows.speaker: Baghawi and Zamakhshari
rows.claim: The statement that their brother stole refers to the King's cup being found in Benjamin's bag.
rows.anchor: the finding of the King's cup in Benjamin's bag (Baghawi and Zamakhshari)

rows.speaker: Zamakhshari
rows.claim: The brothers mean that when they pledged to protect Benjamin, they could not know he would steal because that lay beyond their perception.
rows.anchor: we did not know that he would steal" (Zamakhshari)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jacob's hope that God would bring them all back includes Benjamin, the eldest son left in Egypt, and Joseph, whose death Jacob had never fully accepted.
rows.anchor: Benjamin and the eldest son (who had remained in Egypt) as well as Joseph

rows.speaker: Razi
rows.claim: Razi explains that Jacob's eyes became dim with tears, rather than reading white as literal blindness.
rows.anchor: "white": i.e., dim with the tears that filled them (Razi)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jacob's grief for Joseph was sharpest because he did not know whether Joseph was alive or dead, unlike the other two lost sons.
rows.anchor: his grief for Joseph was the most acute because he was the only one of the three of whom Jacob did not know

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's exclusive judgment and the duty to trust Him are the surah's twin underlying ideas, which Jacob impresses on his sons.
rows.anchor: the twin ideas which underlie the whole of this surah, and which Jacob now seeks to impress upon his sons

rows.speaker: Razi and Ibn Kathir
rows.claim: Remembering Joseph's prophetic dream and Jacob's conviction that God had chosen him renewed Jacob's hope that Joseph was alive, explaining his instruction to search.
rows.anchor: Joseph is still alive (Razi and Ibn Kathir)

rows.speaker: Ibn 'Abbas
rows.claim: Most commentators, especially Ibn Abbas as cited by Tabari, take rawh here as synonymous with rahmah, grace or mercy.
rows.anchor: According to most of the commentators, especially Ibn 'Abbas (as quoted by Tabari and others), the term rawh is here synonymous with rahmah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because rawh is linked to breath or spirit and to relief from grief, Asad prefers life-giving mercy as the rendering.
rows.anchor: the most appropriate rendering would seem to be "life-giving mercy"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The scanty merchandise was goods the brothers planned to barter for grain, as in note 60.
rows.anchor: goods which they intended to barter for grain (see note 60 above)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording is literally know, as in the earlier phrase Asad explains as remembrance in verse 80.
rows.anchor: Lit., "know" (see note 81)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: By naming himself with Benjamin, Joseph may hint at his brothers' early envy and hatred of Rachel's two sons.
rows.anchor: By coupling his own name with that of Benjamin he possibly hinted at his brothers' early envy and hatred of the two sons of Rachel

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, Benjamin may be named because the brothers readily accepted the evidence of his guilt.
rows.anchor: alternatively, the mention of Benjamin may have been due to the readiness with which they accepted the "evidence" of the latter's guilt (verse 77)

rows.speaker: Razi
rows.claim: Razi says Jacob need not have become literally blind: learning Joseph was alive could end his weeping and the dimness caused by prolonged unhappiness and tears.
rows.anchor: thus may be summed up Razi's explanation of the above sentence

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Arabic wajh, literally face, can mean a person's whole being, so the phrase may mean lay the tunic before Jacob.
rows.anchor: the term wajh (lit., "face") is often used in classical Arabic to denote, metonymically, one's whole personality, or whole being

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad links Jacob's declaration in verse 96 to his earlier statement that he knew from God what his sons did not.
rows.anchor: See verse 86 above.

none: source text is cut off mid-word at "foster-"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad takes al-arsh as throne in a metaphorical sense.
rows.anchor: Lit., "onto the throne (al-'arsh)", in the metaphorical sense of this word

rows.speaker: 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas, as quoted by Razi, says before Him refers to God because Joseph could not have allowed his parents to prostrate before him.
rows.anchor: According to 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas (as quoted by Razi), the personal pronoun in "before Him" relates to God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph's childhood dream was fulfilled through his elevated dignity and his family's arrival from Canaan to Egypt for his sake, not by an exact replay of the dream.
rows.anchor: The fulfilment of Joseph's childhood dream consisted in the high dignity with which he was now invested

rows.speaker: Razi
rows.claim: Razi's reasoning is that a dream's fulfillment need not exactly reproduce the dream's symbolic scene of the eleven stars, sun, and moon prostrating.
rows.anchor: no reasonable person can expect that the fulfilment of a dream should be an exact replica of the dream itself" (Razi
